messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Moana had always been a bright and ambitious young woman, with a promising career as an auditor ahead of her. But everything changed when she was stalked by a former acquaintance. The experience left her feeling constantly on edge, as if she was walking around with a target on her back. As the days turned into weeks, Moana began to withdraw from social interactions and situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. She stopped going out with friends, quit her book club, and even started avoiding family gatherings. When asked about it, she explained that she just didn't see the point of putting herself out there anymore - after all, what was the use when the world was such a dangerous place? Her loved ones tried to reassure her, but Moana had come to believe that her life had been irreparably destroyed by the trauma. The thought echoed in her mind like a mantra: "My life has been destroyed." Moana's work began to suffer as well. As an auditor, she was required to visit clients at their offices, but now she found herself hypervigilant whenever she stepped out of her own apartment. She would scan the streets for familiar faces, constantly checking over her shoulder, and wondering if she was being watched. Her colleagues noticed a change in her behavior and asked if everything was okay, but Moana just shrugged it off, saying she was "just being cautious". Deep down, however, she knew that this wasn't just about caution - she had to be on guard all the time because that's what the world demanded. As time passed, Moana started to internalize her negative appraisals. She began to tell herself that she deserved to suffer because of what happened - that somehow, she must have brought it upon herself. This self-punishing narrative played in the background of her mind like a perpetual hum, influencing every decision she made and every interaction she had. When faced with situations that might bring her joy or relief, Moana found herself avoiding them altogether. Why bother trying to feel better when the world was just going to hurt her again? Her loved ones grew increasingly worried about her, but Moana couldn't shake off the conviction that she was somehow broken beyond repair. Lately, things had come to a head. Moana's boss called her into his office, concerned about her performance and her increasing isolation from colleagues. He offered her support and resources, but Moana just felt overwhelmed by the thought of having to open up about her experiences again. It was then that she realized she needed professional help - not just to manage her symptoms, but to try and rebuild a sense of self-worth that had been shattered by the trauma. As she sat in his office, listening to his words of encouragement, Moana felt a glimmer of hope for the first time in months. Maybe, just maybe, she could learn to let go of some of that hypervigilance and start living again - but the thought was terrifying, because what if the world really was as dangerous as she believed it to be?
